summary: Specifies a simple, generic RTP payload format for carrying any non-multiplexed MPEG-4 elementary stream. MPEG-4 compresses audio-visual content into elementary streams, and this format lets them travel over RTP. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Video files are squashed into streams. This gives a way to cut those streams into small packets for sending over the Internet, like putting a long scroll into a series of envelopes.

questions: how to stream mpeg-4 elementary streams
what is an access unit in mpeg-4
subtitle: A configurable RTP payload format for carrying any MPEG-4 elementary stream, with fragmentation and optional interleaving.

tldr.problem: MPEG-4 compresses audio and video into elementary streams made of Access Units, and these need a generic way to travel over RTP without losing timing or ordering.
tldr.mechanism: The payload has three sections (AU headers, auxiliary data, Access Unit data) whose fields are switched on and sized by MIME format parameters, and named modes pin down common configurations.
tldr.outcome: It supports concatenating, fragmenting and interleaving Access Units. It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5691.

today: RFC 3640 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5691, so the two should be read together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPEG-4 compresses audio-visual data into elementary streams, each a sequence of Access Units (AUs), such as one audio frame or one video picture. This RFC defines a general, configurable RTP payload for any non-multiplexed MPEG-4 stream: audio (including speech), video, and systems streams such as BIFS, OCI, OD and IPMP.

Some system streams carry crucial information whose loss cannot be tolerated, while RTP does not guarantee delivery. The RFC therefore adds stream-state signalling so a receiver can detect likely loss and stop decoding until the next random access point. It also suggests measures such as retransmission or forward error correction used with care for congestion control, or carrying RTP over TCP.

More specific formats exist, for example RFC 3016 for MPEG-4 video. This format can be configured to be nearly identical to RFC 3016 for the video configurations that RFC recommends.
sections.eli5: Some pieces of a show are so important that if one goes missing the picture breaks. This memo adds a way to notice that and wait for a safe restart point.

sections.title: Access Units: Concatenating and Fragmenting
sections.content:
An Access Unit is the smallest piece of an MPEG stream that gets its own timing. Access Units are octet-aligned, so up to 7 zero bits are added at the end if needed.

Concatenation: several AUs can share one RTP packet, which is especially useful for audio. The RFC's example is AAC stereo at 64 kbits/sec, where frames average about 200 octets, so about 7 fit in a 1500-octet MTU. When AU sizes are constant, the size is given once out of band; when they vary, each AU gets an in-band size field. Every AU in a packet MUST be complete, and an AU MUST NOT be repeated in other packets.

Fragmentation: very large AUs can be split over several packets. A packet carries either one or more complete AUs or a single fragment of one AU, never fragments of several. Fragments of one AU share a timestamp but have different sequence numbers, and the marker bit is 1 on the last fragment.
sections.eli5: Small pieces can share one envelope, while one huge piece is cut into several envelopes. But an envelope never mixes a cut piece with other pieces.

sections.title: Structure of the Payload
sections.content:
After the RTP header, the payload has three octet-aligned sections. The AU Header Section and the Auxiliary Section may be empty. The Access Unit Data Section MUST NOT be empty and holds either one fragment of an AU or one or more complete AUs, in decoding order.

Which fields exist, and how many bits each takes, is set by MIME format parameters. A length of zero means the field is absent, so parsing a payload requires knowing those parameters. They normally arrive in SDP, but other means are allowed.

The Auxiliary Section holds an auxiliary-data-size field followed by auxiliary data whose format is not defined here. It MUST NOT be sent until its format and signalling have been specified in a future RFC, and receivers that do not understand it MUST skip it. The RFC also advises that the size and number of AUs should keep the packet within the path MTU.
sections.eli5: Each packet is a lunchbox with up to three compartments: a label list, an optional extras pocket, and the food itself. The food compartment is never empty.

sections.title: The AU Header Section
sections.content:
When present, the section starts with a two-octet AU-headers-length giving the length in bits of the AU headers that follow (without padding), then one AU-header per AU in the same order as the data, bit-wise concatenated, with up to 7 zero padding bits to reach an octet boundary.

An AU-header can contain, in this order: AU-size, AU-Index (first header) or AU-Index-delta (later headers), CTS-flag, CTS-delta, DTS-flag, DTS-delta, RAP-flag and Stream-state. The lengths come from MIME parameters; a parameter left at its default of zero removes the field.

  • AU-size is the size of the whole AU in octets, even for a fragment.
  • AU-Index numbers AUs; each later AU is coded as AU-Index(n) = AU-Index(n-1) + AU-Index-delta(n) + 1. A delta above 0 means interleaving is used.
  • CTS-delta and DTS-delta are 2's complement offsets from the RTP timestamp and from the CTS.
  • RAP-flag set to 1 marks a random access point.
  • Stream-state is a modulo counter, incremented by one when the state of a system stream changes.
sections.eli5: Each piece gets a small tag with its size, its place in line, optional clock times, and a flag saying it is a safe place to start watching.

sections.title: RTP Header Use, Timestamps and Crucial Data
sections.content:
The RTP timestamp carries the sampling instant of the first AU in the packet, which equals the MPEG-4 composition time stamp (CTS). The clock rate MUST be given with rtpmap: for audio it SHOULD equal the audio sampling rate, and for video 90 kHz is RECOMMENDED. The marker bit is 1 when the packet holds the final fragment of an AU or complete AUs. Timestamps for later AUs can be calculated for constant frame rates, or carried as deltas in the AU headers. A decoding time stamp (DTS) can also be carried for streams with bi-directional coding.

For MPEG-4 system streams, a crucial AU is one whose loss breaks later AUs. At each crucial AU the stream state changes. If an AU may have been lost and the state changed, the stream is considered corrupted until the next random access point. Decoders follow three rules: a RAP AU with a state change MUST be decoded; a RAP AU without a state change is decoded only if the stream is corrupted; a non-RAP AU is decoded unless the stream is corrupted.
sections.eli5: If an important instruction is lost, the later ones make no sense. So the receiver pauses until it reaches a point where it can safely start again.

sections.title: Interleaving and the De-interleave Buffer
sections.content:
Unless the signalled mode prohibits it, a sender MAY interleave AUs so that one lost packet leaves gaps in different places rather than one run of missing AUs. The sender needs to tell the receiver only how much buffer to allocate; the receiver reads each AU's index and puts it in the right place. Receivers that support an interleaving mode MUST be able to decode interleaved AUs.

If AUs have constant duration, signalled with constantDuration, the receiver rebuilds timing from the RTP timestamp and AU-Index-delta, and AU-Index MUST be 0. For variable durations, constantDuration MUST NOT be present, AU-Index carries the ordering and CTS-delta MUST be coded for non-first AUs.

Receivers must put early AUs aside in a de-interleave buffer. The sender MUST signal a maxDisplacement value, the maximum displacement in time of an AU. The buffer size is estimated as maxDisplacement times the maximum bit rate divided by the RTP clock frequency. If that underestimates the need, the sender MUST also signal de-interleaveBufferSize. In the RFC's 3-AU example the buffer holds at most 4 AUs, and the maximum displacement is 5 AU periods.
sections.eli5: If you deal playing cards out of order, you keep early cards in your hand until the missing ones arrive. The hand-size you need is what the sender tells you.

sections.title: MIME Parameters and Modes
sections.content:
The MIME subtype is mpeg4-generic, and the type is video, audio or application depending on the stream. Required parameters are streamType, profile-level-id, config and mode. Optional ones include constantSize, constantDuration, maxDisplacement, de-interleaveBufferSize, sizeLength, indexLength, indexDeltaLength, CTSDeltaLength, DTSDeltaLength, randomAccessIndication, streamStateIndication and auxiliaryDataSizeLength. In SDP they go on an a=fmtp line as semicolon-separated name=value pairs.

A mode fixes a payload configuration so simple receivers need not parse every parameter. The mode MUST be signalled. This RFC defines five. New modes can be defined by later RFCs, MUST be registered with IANA, and MUST NOT change default parameter values.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, sender and receiver swap a settings sheet. Modes are ready-made settings sheets for common cases like voice or music.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The payload inherits RTP's security considerations. Confidentiality comes from encryption, which can be applied to the compressed data. The packet-handling work of this format does not vary enough to create a denial-of-service risk.

The larger risk is non-compliant MPEG-4 content. Injected streams can overload decoder buffers and crash a receiver, and MPEG-4 systems streams can carry commands and programmatic content such as MPEG-J (Java) and scripts. Senders SHOULD ensure content is MPEG compliant, receivers should guard against bad content, and authentication can validate the sender. Implementations that support MPEG-4 scripts MUST limit them to the single presentation they belong to, and network access by scripts MUST be restricted to downloading media.
sections.eli5: A broken or sneaky stream could confuse the player. So senders should send only proper streams, and players should not let a show's scripts wander outside the show.

layers.label: RTP Header
layers.detail: Timestamp is the CTS of the first AU

layers.label: AU Header Section
layers.detail: AU-headers-length plus one AU-header per AU; may be empty

layers.label: Auxiliary Section
layers.detail: Size field plus auxiliary data; may be empty

layers.label: Access Unit Data Section
layers.detail: One fragment or one or more complete AUs; never empty

data.title: 3 AUs per packet, interleaving group length 9
data.code:
RTP packet(0):  AU(0),  AU(3),  AU(6)
RTP packet(1):  AU(1),  AU(4),  AU(7)
RTP packet(2):  AU(2),  AU(5),  AU(8)
RTP packet(3):  AU(9),  AU(12), AU(15)
RTP packet(4):  AU(10), AU(13), AU(16)

items.label: mode=generic
items.desc: Any MPEG-4 stream; full flexibility of the format.

items.label: mode=CELP-cbr
items.desc: Fixed-size CELP frames; no interleaving; AU Header and Auxiliary Sections empty.

items.label: mode=CELP-vbr
items.desc: Variable-size CELP frames; optional interleaving; one-octet AU-header (6-bit size, 2-bit index).

items.label: mode=AAC-lbr
items.desc: AAC frames up to 63 octets; interleaving allowed; no fragmentation.

items.label: mode=AAC-hbr
items.desc: AAC frames up to 8191 octets; 13-bit size and 3-bit index; fragmentation allowed.
